item.title: A Sharp Additive Bound for the Threshold Rule in Repeated Rent-or-Buy
item.description: arXiv:2611.06955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by context management in LLM agents, we study a repeated rent-or-buy model with schedule-independent history growth and a fixed reset price $K$, a discrete form of dynamic TCP acknowledgment: every call pays as rent the history accumulated since the last reset, and a reset clears it. The classical threshold rule is $2$-competitive, and no deterministic rule guarantees a smaller ratio. We show that, measured additively, its loss is governed by the changes in the growth: if the growth is constant on $P$ runs, the threshold rule, knowing neither the runs nor the horizon, pays at most $(2P-1)K$ more than the optimal schedule chosen with hindsight, and the coefficient $2P-1$ is sharp. If the growth is only within a factor $1+\varepsilon$ of $P$ runs, the bound holds up to a factor $1+\varepsilon$ and an extra $\varepsilon K$. The proof is a potential argument built from the relative value functions of the single-rate problems. On two runs no deterministic rule guarantees a loss below $2K$. A rule that also resets when the growth decreases guarantees $2K$, while the threshold rule can lose arbitrarily close to $3K$.
item.dc:creator: Vasco Schiavo

item.title: An Integrality-Gap Lower Bound of 1.2325 for Minimum Multiway Cut
item.description: arXiv:2611.06957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the integrality gap of the C\u{a}linescu-Karloff-Rabani relaxation for Minimum Multiway Cut is at least $1.2325$ when the number of terminals is large. By a result of Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008), it is therefore NP-hard, under the Unique Games Conjecture, to approximate Minimum Multiway Cut within a factor of $1.2325$. This improves the previously best known lower bound of $1.20016$ due to B\'erczi, Chandrasekaran, Kir\'aly, and Madan (2020).
item.dc:creator: Dimitar Chakarov, Yury Makarychev

item.title: Polynomial Lower Bounds for Steiner Shortcuts via Test Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.07043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Steiner shortcut problem asks whether every directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges admits an augmentation $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+o(1)}$ edges such that $G_+$ has the same reachability structure as $G$ (i.e. for all $s,t\in V$, $s$ reaches $t$ in $G$ iff $s$ reaches $t$ in $G_+$), and the diameter of $G_{+}$ is $m^{o(1)}$. This is a core combinatorial question underlying many reachability algorithms in the dynamic, streaming, and CONGEST models, and all parallel algorithms with almost-linear work and sublinear depth. A sequence of works ruled out such a shortcut $G_{+}$ in the non-Steiner setting where $V_{+}=\emptyset$. However, as recently shown by Bernstein et al. [STOC '26], all known non-Steiner lower-bound constructions fail once Steiner vertices $V_{+}$ are allowed. This paper rules out almost-optimal Steiner shortcuts: we show an infinite family of graphs $G=(V,E)$ with the property that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, a Steiner shortcut $G_{+}=(V\cup V_{+},E\cup E_{+})$ with $m^{1+\varepsilon}$ edges must have diameter at least $n^{1/56-O(\varepsilon)}$. Our construction strengthens the standard non-Steiner lower-bound framework via an additional structure that allows Steiner vertices to be replaced by original vertices; we can then reduce back to the standard arguments without Steiner vertices. This new structure is achieved via a new general strategy based on test functions, which is quite flexible and can potentially be extended to applications beyond our work. We also generalize our lower bound to exact Steiner hopsets in undirected graphs and to depth reduction for monotone circuits. The latter significantly strengthens the classical lower bound based on Sylvester matrices.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Bernstein, Henry Fleischmann, Bernhard Haeupler, Gary Hoppenworth, Thatchaphol Saranurak

item.title: $L_1$ versus $L_2$ Clustering: When Does the Choice of Norm Matter?
item.description: arXiv:2611.07248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how well approximation guarantees for clustering under one norm translate into guarantees under another. Specifically, we compare $k$-clustering in $\mathbb{R}^d$ under the $L_1$ and $L_2$ objectives, defined as the sums of Manhattan and Euclidean distances, respectively. In the worst case, the elementary relationship between these norms yields a $\sqrt{d}$ approximation bound, which is already tight for $k=2$. We therefore investigate whether stronger guarantees are possible in a natural average-case model, where the dataset is arbitrary but the coordinate system is chosen uniformly at random among all orthonormal bases. Our main result shows that, when $d=\Omega(\log k)$, with high probability over the random rotation, any $\beta$-approximate $L_1$ clustering, with optimally chosen centers for its clusters, is also an $O(\beta)$-approximation under the $L_2$ objective. We also establish an expected approximation ratio of $O(\beta\min\{\sqrt{d},k^{2/d}\})$, yielding a dimension-independent bound of $O(\beta\sqrt{\log k/\log\log k})$. We obtain analogous guarantees in the reverse direction, from $L_2$ to $L_1$. We complement these results with lower bounds of $\Omega(\min\{\sqrt{d},k^{1/d}\})$ in both directions, showing that our dimension-independent guarantees have asymptotically optimal dependence on $k$ for constant $\beta$. Our proofs overcome the dependence of the algorithm's output on the random rotation using geometric projection arguments and small Euclidean coresets. In particular, our results provide guarantees for existing clustering algorithms without requiring their redesign.
item.dc:creator: Nick Gravin, Jianhao Jia

item.title: Quadratic-Time Barriers from Self-Referential SAT
item.description: arXiv:2611.07308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the self-referential $K$-SAT exhaustive-search hypothesis (SRK-ESH), no uniform deterministic algorithm computes exact longest common subsequence or standard edit distance on binary strings in $O(n^{2-\eta})$ time for any fixed $\eta>0$, where $n$ is the longer sequence length. The same exclusion holds for one-dimensional dynamic time warping on $\{0,1,2,4,8\}$ with absolute-difference cost and for five-symbol dynamic time warping with the discrete metric. We derive Orthogonal Vectors hardness in polylogarithmic dimension by splitting the variables of the logarithmic-width source formula into two halves. Existing sequence reductions have polynomial overhead in the dimension. Their output lengths and construction times allow a fixed saving in the target exponent to yield a fixed proportional saving in the source exponent.
item.dc:creator: Guangyan Zhou

item.title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
item.description: arXiv:2611.07313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant. It uses $\poly(p,\ell)$ working space outside the oracle, and all oracle queries have rank $N$ and $\poly(p,\ell)$ bit complexity. For $p=2$, the reduction transfers polynomial-space exact SVP algorithms to exact CVP with $2^{O(N)}\poly(\ell)$ time overhead. Instantiating it with the SVP algorithms of Kannan and of Feng, Gao and Liu yields randomized polynomial-space CVP algorithms running in time $N^{N/(2e)+o(N)}$ and $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$, respectively. For every fixed integer $p\ge3$, the same reduction yields exact $\ell_p$-CVP algorithms for arbitrary rational targets either in randomized time and space $2^{O(N)}$, or in randomized time $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$ and polynomial space. These algorithmic bounds are up to polynomial factors in $\ell$. The reduction performs local search sequentially over the cosets of \(2L\), where \(L\) is the input lattice, while tracking the excess of the current objective value over the optimum. Within a coset containing a closest vector, midpoint inequalities bound the unknown correction in terms of this excess, which in turn allows us to construct many short corrections that reduce the excess bound by a factor of four. A counting argument shows that these improving corrections form a sufficiently large fraction of the lattice points in a known search region, and a sparsification-based sampler assigns sufficiently large probability to every nonzero vector in that region, using at most one SVP call per sample. For \(p\ge3\), the same framework is extended using a diagonal weighted norm computed from the current point.
item.dc:creator: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Hyung Tae Lee

item.title: GreedTok is a Constant-Factor Approximation for Partition-Cover Tokenization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GreedTok (Lim, Tan, Choo and Lauw, NeurIPS 2025) builds a tokenizer vocabulary greedily for the partition-cover objective: choose $k$ tokens so as to maximize the number of adjacent character pairs merged when the corpus is segmented optimally. The objective is neither submodular nor supermodular, so the classical $1-1/e$ analysis does not apply, and a worst-case guarantee was left open. We prove that GreedTok is a constant-factor approximation: on every corpus and for every budget $k$ it achieves at least $0.2752$ of the optimum, and it is optimal for $k=1$. The bound holds for both the exact greedy loop and the lazy priority-queue loop of the published algorithm and its code. The key ingredient is a shift lemma: if two occurrences of a not-yet-chosen token overlap and both are still usable, they offer exactly the same gain, so GreedTok's left-to-right scoring loses nothing when occurrences collide. A per-occurrence charging argument, with window distributions certified in exact arithmetic or given in closed form, completes the proof. In the other direction, we construct corpora on which GreedTok, with adversarial tie-breaking, achieves at most a fraction of the optimum tending to $(7-\ln 2)/12\approx0.5256$ (below $0.5380$ when every greedy choice is unique). Finally, we show that the objective is NP-hard to approximate within $1-1/31580$, to our knowledge the first inapproximability result for it.
item.dc:creator: Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju

item.title: Constant-Factor Approximations for the Biased Traveling Salesman Problem and Its Path Variant
item.description: arXiv:2611.07348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a fundamental problem in combinatorial optimization that asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in a complete undirected graph with $N$ vertices, where edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality. The biased TSP (BTSP) is a natural generalization of the metric TSP, in which the vertex set is partitioned into $k$ subsets: edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality within each subset, while edges crossing the subsets may violate the triangle inequality by a certain bias factor. This model captures scenarios in which distances are metric only locally but may be distorted across different regions or types of vertices. In this paper, we study approximation algorithms for the BTSP and its path variant, the biased traveling salesman path problem (BTSPP), which asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian path. Previously, constant-factor approximation algorithms were known only for the case $k=2$. Whether the BTSP and the BTSPP admit constant-factor approximation algorithms for any fixed integer $k>2$ has remained an open question. We resolve this question affirmatively. We show that both the BTSP and the BTSPP admit $O(k)$-approximation algorithms with running time $N^{O(2^k k!)}$. Moreover, for the BTSPP with $k=2$, we propose an improved $(\alpha+2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm, where $\alpha<3/2-10^{-34}$ is the best-known approximation ratio for the metric TSP, improving upon the previous ratio of $4$
item.dc:creator: Jingyang Zhao, Jason William Setiawan, Uman Khalid, Chaoning Zhang, Een-Kee Hong, Hyundong Shin

item.title: Constant-Factor Approximation Algorithms for Weighted Budgeted Multisensor Sweep Coverage
item.description: arXiv:2611.07355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sweep coverage requires each point of interest (PoI) to be revisited by some mobile sensor at least once during every sweep period, and it underlies persistent patrolling, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection. Given a set of $N$ PoIs, each associated with a nonnegative weight representing its importance, the weighted budgeted sweep coverage problem (WB-SCP) seeks routing trajectories for a budget of $M\leq N$ identical mobile sensors with a common maximum speed to maximize the total weight of the sweep-covered PoIs. For the unweighted special case in which every PoI has unit weight, the first constant-factor approximation algorithm achieves a ratio of $0.0116-O(\varepsilon)$ for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, and whether the WB-SCP itself admits such an algorithm has remained open. In this paper, we resolve this open question by proposing two constant-factor approximation algorithms for the WB-SCP. The first converts any bifactor $(\alpha,\beta)$-approximation algorithm into a $\beta/(2\alpha)$-approximation algorithm, yielding a ratio of $1/16=0.0625$. The second builds on a greedy maximum-coverage framework and improves the ratio to $1-e^{-1/2}-\varepsilon$ for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Both algorithms also improve the best-known ratio for the unweighted case, and the second extends to heterogeneous sensors with different speeds while preserving the same guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Jingyang Zhao, Jason William Setiawan, Uman Khalid, Chaoning Zhang, Een-Kee Hong, Hyundong Shin

item.title: A Simple Discrete Newton Method for the Quickest Transshipment Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.07369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quickest transshipment problem is a problem defined in a dynamic network with multiple sources and multiple sinks. The goal of this problem is to send all the supplies from sources to sinks as quickly as possible. It is known that this problem can be solved in polynomial time. In particular, Schl\"oter, Skutella, and Tran proposed a strongly polynomial-time discrete Newton method for this problem. In this paper, we propose a simple polynomial-time discrete Newton method for the quickest transshipment problem.
item.dc:creator: Naoyuki Kamiyama

item.title: Sharp Limits of Graph-Based Nearest Neighbor Search on the Sphere
item.description: arXiv:2611.07603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the degree needed for greedy graph search to find the exact nearest neighbor from every starting point on graphs of $n$ independent data points on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^d$. For uniform data, we determine an explicit sublinear degree threshold when $d$ is proportional to $\log n$, and the threshold $2^{d/2+o(d)}$ in the dense regime $\sqrt{\log n}\ll d\ll\log n$. Above these thresholds by fixed exponent gaps, the nearest-neighbor graph succeeds from every entry for most uniform queries with high probability, with evaluation cost on the same exponential scale as its degree. Matching lower bounds hold for every graph designed after observing the sample. For nonuniform data in the dense regime, local density variation shifts the critical degree. Under explicit local regularity conditions and within a specified range of density variation, we derive a sharp worst-case degree curve and show that the nearest-neighbor graph attains it. We construct sampling densities and query distributions for which, with high probability, every graph whose degree lies below this curve by a fixed exponent gap has failing entries for most queries. Allowing fresh uniform random entries reduces the cost of exact recovery. For uniform data in the dense regime, we determine the exact exponent for the number of distinct distance evaluations over a range of degrees below the critical threshold. Independent restarts on a single graph joining points within a prescribed radius attain this exponent with high probability. Matching lower bounds hold for adaptive local exploration on threshold and nearest-neighbor graphs using entries independent of the data. Optimizing within this degree range lowers the exponent from $\frac12\log2\approx0.347$ for success from every entry to approximately $0.243$.
item.dc:creator: Kejing Lu

item.title: Approximate Hamming Convolution via Rectangular Matrix Multiplication
item.description: arXiv:2611.07622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study $(1 \pm \epsilon)$-approximate text-to-pattern Hamming distance: given a length-$N$ pattern and a length-$2N$ text, compute the Hamming distance at every alignment to relative error $\epsilon$. For every fixed $a \ge 0$ and $\epsilon = N^{-a}$, we give a randomized algorithm with simultaneous high-probability correctness on a logarithmic-word RAM and expected running time $\widetilde{O}(N^{\omega(4a)/2})$, where $\widetilde{O}$ suppresses subpolynomial factors and $\omega(k)$ is the exponent for multiplying an $n \times n^k$ matrix by an $n^k \times n$ matrix. With a recent rectangular bound, this improves the published bounds [CGK+20, FKN26] for $1/12 < a < (3 + \sqrt{3})/16$. In particular, the algorithm runs in expected time $\widetilde{O}(N)$ for $0 \le a \le 1/8$, extending the previous near-linear guarantee through $a = 1/12$.
item.dc:creator: Przemyslaw Uznanski

item.title: Adversarially Robust Streaming Algorithms for $(k, z)$-Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2611.07678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We design adversarially robust algorithms for dynamic geometric streams that $(1 + \epsilon)$-approximate $k$-Median and $k$-Means in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$, using $\tilde{O}(kd \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1}))$ space. This result significantly improves a recent $O(d\log n)$-approximation for $k$-Median [Gribelyuk, Lin, Woodruff, Yu, and Zhou, FOCS 2026], and is furthermore the first algorithm whose space is linear in $kd$, even in the oblivious (non-adaptive) setting. We develop several new techniques which may be of independent interest, including a new data-oblivious Euclidean primitive called hierarchical Lipschitz assignment, a robust dimensionality reduction for clustering, and a robust streaming algorithm for inner-product queries.
item.dc:creator: Chengzhi Guo, Shaofeng H. C. Jiang, Robert Krauthgamer, David P. Woodruff, Shenghao Xie, Samson Zhou

item.title: Quasi-polynomial-sized vertex multicut-mimicking networks and kernelization for Vertex Multiway Cut
item.description: arXiv:2611.07880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give deterministic polynomial-time constructions of vertex multicut-mimicking networks of quasi-polynomial size. Given a graph G, a terminal set T, and a positive integer c, our algorithm constructs a graph with |T|^7 c^{O( log c ) } vertices that preserves every minimum vertex multiway cut value of at most c, for every partition of the terminals. Setting c=|T| gives an exact vertex multicut-mimicking network with |T|^{O( log |T| ) } vertices, resolving an open question of Wahlstr\"om [ACM Transactions on Algorithms 2022], who showed a bound of \kappa^{O( log^3 \kappa)} for the edge multicut-mimicking variant, where \kappa:= \sum_{t \in T} |N_G(t)| is the capacity of the terminal set, which was later improved to \kappa^{O( log^2 \kappa)} by Anand, Lee, Li and Saranurak [STOC 2024]. As applications of our vertex multicut-mimicking network, we obtain deterministic kernels of size k^{O( log k )} for Vertex Multiway Cut, p^{O(1)} k^{O(log k)} for Vertex Multicut with p requests and |\Gamma|^{O(1)} k^{O( log k)} for Group Feedback Vertex Set, where k is the deletion budget and \Gamma is a finite group. Our first kernelization result, in particular, resolves an open question by Wahlstr\"om [ACM Transactions on Algorithms 2022], which was reiterated in a recent survey on kernelization by Jansen [Computer Science Reviews 2026]. Also, to the best of our knowledge, our kernel for Vertex Multicut is the first one whose size is completely polynomial in p and (quasi-polynomial) super-polynomial only in k. Finally, again using our vertex multicut-mimicking network for graphs, we obtain a hyperedge multicut-mimicking network for hypergraphs, which preserves hypergraph edge-multicuts of size up to c, of size |T|^{O(1)} c^{O(log c)}. Our result removes the dependence on the rank of the hypergraph from the exponent of the size bound, that existed in prior work.
item.dc:creator: Eduard Eiben, Roohani Sharma, Magnus Wahlstr\"om

item.title: Tight Worst-Case Completion-Time Bounds for Dominant Resource Fairness
item.description: arXiv:2611.07905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) is an influential policy for sharing multiple resources among jobs with heterogeneous demands. It combines sharing incentive, strategy-proofness, envy-freeness, and Pareto efficiency, making it particularly attractive for shared computing systems. DRF has been implemented in major resource-management frameworks, including Apache Mesos and Hadoop YARN. DRF is also nonclairvoyant: it requires no advance knowledge of job sizes, making it practical when processing requirements are difficult to predict. This motivates understanding its completion-time performance relative to an optimal schedule that knows all job sizes. However, elementary arguments can only give an $\Omega(\sqrt D)$ lower bound and an $O(D)$ upper bound for total completion time, where $D$ is the number of resource types. In this paper, we close this gap by proving that DRF is $\Theta(\sqrt D)$-competitive. More generally, for every fixed real $q\geq1$, we show that DRF is $\Theta(D^{1/(q+1)})$-competitive for the $\ell_q$ norm of completion times, with larger $q$ placing greater emphasis on late-finishing jobs. These bounds hold with arbitrary release times. We also give a refined analysis of total completion time for small $D$.
item.dc:creator: Mugen Blue, Sungjin Im, Alexander Lindermayr

item.title: Solving Linear Programs in the Matrix Multiplication Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.07980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a randomized algorithm for feasible bounded-box linear programs with $n$ variables and $d\le n=O(d)$ linearly independent equality constraints. For additive accuracy $\epsilon$, its expected running time is $O((n^\omega+n^2\log n)\log(1/\epsilon))$, where $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. This answers the matrix-multiplication-time open question posted in Song's Ph.D. thesis [Son19] in this setting.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song

item.title: Sum-of-Squares Refutation Implies Planted Recovery for Semirandom CSPs
item.description: arXiv:2611.08114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a $n^{O(\ell)}$-time algorithm for solving semirandom planted instances of a $k$-ary Boolean constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) with $m \gtrsim \left(\frac{n}{\ell}\right)^{k/2} \ell \, \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ constraints, for any choice of the runtime parameter $\ell$. Up to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factors, this matches the known runtime vs.\ number of constraints trade-off for refuting semirandom CSPs, as well as the trade-off for solving fully random planted CSPs. Prior work on designing algorithms for semirandom CSPs follows a high-level blueprint of decomposing the constraint hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ of the instance into pieces, each with an explicit pseudorandom property that allows the standard algorithm for random CSPs to succeed on every piece. We depart considerably from this framework and instead implicitly \emph{learn} such a decomposition, without appealing directly to explicit properties such as expansion. More generally, we construct such a learning algorithm from the assumption that semirandom $k$-XOR has Sum-of-Squares certificates of refutation. This yields the broader implication that any Sum-of-Squares refutation algorithm for semirandom $k$-XOR gives a corresponding algorithm for solving semirandom planted CSPs, and instantiating this reduction with known Sum-of-Squares algorithms for refuting semirandom $k$-XOR gives our main algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reduction from search to refutation for (semi)random CSPs.
item.dc:creator: Arpon Basu, Andrew D. Lin, Peter Manohar

item.title: Counting over Unbreakable Decompositions: A Single-Exponential Parameterized Algorithm for Minimum Bisection
item.description: arXiv:2611.08202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Minimum Bisection problem asks whether an $n$-vertex graph can be split into two halves with at most $k$ edges between them. We give a single exponential time algorithm for minimum bisection, running in time $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$. This improves the previous bound of $2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}$ due to Cygan, Komosa, Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, Saurabh, and Wahlstr\"om (TALG 2021). Our algorithm counts solutions instead of only finding if one exists. We show that our dynamic program can be implemented on top of an unbreakable decomposition using algebraic techniques. Along the way, we compute in time $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$ a tree decomposition with adhesions of size at most $2k$ whose bags are $(3k,k)$-edge-unbreakable inside their own subtrees.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Anand, Evangelos Kipouridis, Karol W\k{e}grzycki

item.title: All minimum cuts of symmetric submodular functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.08253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compute Cunningham's canonical decomposition of a symmetric submodular function on $n$ elements in $O(n^3)$ time. The decomposition represents all minimum cuts in linear space. For the pair $s,t$ produced by Queyranne's algorithm, we construct in $O(n^2)$ time a digraph representing exactly the minimum $st$-cuts of the function. Using this construction in Chekuri and Xu's decomposition algorithm gives the cubic bound.
item.dc:creator: Chao Xu

item.title: Minimum-Cost $k$-Arborescence Packing in $\tilde O(km+k^4 n)$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.08256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a deterministic, strongly polynomial algorithm running in $\tilde{O}(km+k^4n)$ time that finds $k$ arc-disjoint arborescences of minimum total cost in a directed multigraph with $n$ vertices and $m$ arcs. This significantly improves upon the state of the art for $k \ge 2$ with $k=n^{o(1)}$: the prior fastest weakly polynomial and strongly polynomial algorithms take $\tilde{O}(km\sqrt{n}\log C)$ and $\tilde{O}(kmn)$ time (Gabow and Xu, 1989; Gabow, 1995), respectively. Roughly, our technique can be viewed as a way to apply a linear number of \emph{shortest} augmenting paths in near-linear total time for the special case of the weighted matroid intersection problem between the $k$-fold graphic matroid and the indegree partition matroid. This was previously done in the unweighted case by Gabow (1995), but our approach is different. As an extension, we also obtain a deterministic $\tilde{O}(km^{1+o(1)}+k^5n)$-time algorithm for minimum-cost maximum-cardinality packing of $k$ forests in undirected graphs. In particular, this finds $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees of minimum total cost, if they exist. The previous fastest algorithm takes $\tilde{O}(kn^2+m)$ time (Gabow and Westermann, 1992).
item.dc:creator: Zhaienhe Zhou

item.title: Connectivity in a New Bounded-Space Dynamic Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.08351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new model for dynamic algorithms in which the algorithm has read-only oracle access to a dynamically changing input and random access to its own bounded workspace. It is a dynamic analogue of the time-space tradeoffs for static inputs studied in complexity theory, where only writable memory counts as space. We study dynamic undirected $s$-$t$ connectivity: after every edge update to an $n$-vertex graph, an algorithm with $S$ words of workspace must report whether $s$ and $t$ are connected. The graph is accessed via adjacency list queries (degree, $j$-th neighbor) or adjacency matrix queries. Our algorithms are randomized; our lower bounds hold for randomized algorithms with $cn$ bits of workspace, $c>0$ a small constant ($cn/\log n$ for the worst-case matrix bound). We prove: (1) With adjacency lists, worst-case time $\tilde\Theta(n^2/S^2)$ per insertion is necessary and sufficient for incremental algorithms. (2) With an adjacency matrix, worst-case time $\tilde\Omega(n^2/S)$ per insertion is necessary for incremental algorithms, and sufficient for $S\ge\sqrt{n}$. (3) With amortization, incremental algorithms achieve $\tilde O(n/S)$ time per insertion with adjacency lists and $\tilde O(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, while $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt{n/S})$ and $\tilde\Omega(n\sqrt{n/S})$, respectively, are necessary. (4) Fully dynamic algorithms need amortized time $\tilde\Omega(n/S)$ per update with adjacency lists and $\tilde\Omega(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, even on forests, where both bounds are tight (lists: under bounded degree). Conventional dynamic connectivity admits polylogarithmic update time with $\Omega(n)$ words of space. In contrast, our lower bounds show that polynomial update time is necessary whenever $S\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$, even for a single pair of vertices and even for incremental algorithms with amortized guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Bardiya Aryanfard, Monika Henzinger, John Kuszmaul, Jakob Nogler, Virginia Vassilevska Williams

item.title: A Near-Optimal Generalized Sorting Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.08397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We continue the study of the classic \emph{generalized sorting problem}, a basic variant of ordinary sorting. There are $n$ elements and an (initially hidden) total ordering $\pi$ over them. Unlike in ordinary sorting, however, only \emph{some} comparisons are allowed: those given by the edges of an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ on the elements. How many comparisons are needed to find the total ordering? In ordinary sorting, $\Theta(n \log n)$ comparisons are necessary and sufficient. For generalized sorting, however, the best known upper bound has been $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ since the work of Huang, Kannan, and Khanna (FOCS 2011), who even asked whether the problem might in fact require $n^{1+\Omega(1)}$ comparisons. We show that it does not: we give a randomized algorithm that uses $O(n \log^4 n)$ comparisons in expectation. Thus, up to logarithmic factors, generalized sorting is no harder than ordinary sorting.
item.dc:creator: Sanjeev Khanna, Aaron Putterman, Junkai Song

item.title: Canonical Cut Hierarchy in Almost-Linear Time via Reduction to Max-Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.08466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The canonical cut hierarchy recursively partitions a graph along Tutte-Nash-Williams partitions, choosing the partition with the most number of parts at each step. We give a randomized almost linear-time algorithm for computing this hierarchy in undirected graphs with polynomially bounded capacities via reduction to max-flow. This yields randomized almost linear-time algorithms for computing partition connectivity, strength, both arboricity and fractional arboricity, both integral and fractional spanning tree packing numbers, and implicit representations of the principal partition sequence and a maximum fractional spanning tree packing.
item.dc:creator: Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Harshul Sagar

item.title: Resolving Tusn\'ady's Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.06998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a lower bound of $\Omega_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusn\'ady's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Wengiel

item.title: Stacking Stars: Minimum-Area Packing with and without Rotation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07100v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the problem of packing a given set of polygons into a minimum-area convex container, that is, placing them without overlap so as to minimize the area of their convex hull. Every previously known polynomial-time algorithm with a nontrivial approximation guarantee for packing polygons with arbitrary edge orientations required the polygons to be convex. In fact, an algorithm was not even known when every input polygon was a quadrilateral. We obtain such algorithms for the entire class of star-shaped polygons with unrestricted combinatorial complexity. The stars may be just translated or also rotated. In either case, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm, where $n$ is the number of stars. Likewise, we get $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithms for bin and strip packing, assuming that the diameter of the stars is at most some (small) constant. Previous approximation algorithms for polygon packing focused on convex objects, and the analysis always relied on a density argument, i.e., if the area of the packed objects is at least a fraction $\rho$ of the area of the container, then we have a $(1/\rho)$-approximation. However, star-shaped polygons may need an arbitrarily large area to be packed, even when the total area of the stars approaches $0$ and each star has bounded diameter. This phenomenon prevents the use of density arguments. We instead establish a strong structural property about any packing: Even though the stars can fit together in complicated ways, we can reorganize them into simple stacks, replace these stacks by rectangles, and consider a packing of these rectangles. The rearrangement costs only a factor of $O(\log n)$, which stems from the number of size groups. We complement our algorithms by showing that both the translational and the rotational versions are APX-hard, even for constant complexity stars.
item.dc:creator: Mikkel Abrahamsen, Jacobus Conradi, Arindam Khan, Jack Stade, Sampson Wong, Shuyi Yan, Hanwen Zhang

item.title: Newton Steps are Faster for Linear Complementarity Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear Complementarity Problems (LCPs) with sufficient matrices form a well-studied class of problems, dating back from the foundational works of Cottle and Dantzig (1968). LCPs capture convex quadratic programs, and admit reductions from problems such as discounted stochastic games or mean-payoff games. While the original approach for solving these problems was based on pivoting methods, in their 1991 book, Kojima, Megiddo, Noma, and Yoshise introduced an interior point method (IPM) with running time that is polynomial in the input size, but which depends linearly on a certain parameter called the handicap number of the matrix. Despite the ensuing rich literature on sufficient LCP IPMs, the linear dependence on the handicap number has not been improved since then. We present an IPM whose running time depends on the square root of the handicap number. The algorithm can decrease the duality gap by a constant factor in $O\left(\min\left\{\sqrt{n} (1+\kappa),n^{9/8}\sqrt{1+\kappa}\right\}\right)$ iterations. Curiously, this can already be achieved using standard Newton updates. We analyze the IPM in a norm defined by a local weighting, where centralizing Newton steps quadratically converge to the central path, without any dependence on the handicap number. The weights arise from a characterization by Rump (Linear Algebra and Its Applications, 1997, 1998, 2003) of the sign-real spectral radius and its relation to sufficiency; another ingredient of our proof is a new operator norm characterization of the handicap number. Moreover, the connection to Rump's work also enables us to show coNP-completeness of testing sufficiency, and approximation hardness of the handicap number.
item.dc:creator: Haoyuan Ma, L\'aszl\'o A. V\'egh, Adrian Vladu

item.title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Dependent Graph Classes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08143v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Monadically dependent graph classes are those in which first-order logic cannot encode all graphs. They include all nowhere dense classes and all classes of bounded twin-width. We show that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class. Together with the known hardness result for hereditary classes that are not monadically dependent, this gives a complete characterization of the hereditary graph classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking. This resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory. Our proof combines ideas from structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types). In particular, we show that in monadically dependent classes, tuples of fixed length have only $|U|^{O(1)}$ types of fixed quantifier rank over any set of parameters $U$.
item.dc:creator: Jan Dreier, Nikolas M\"ahlmann, Szymon Toru\'nczyk

item.title: Regret Bounds for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade: Learning the Best Posted-Price Mechanism
item.description: arXiv:2611.08173v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight. We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a $\tilde O(T^{\frac 23})$ regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction. We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde \Theta(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Br\"ustle, Simone Di Gregorio, Federico Fusco, Stefano Leonardi

item.title: Quantum Advantage with Sign-Free Proofs: An Oracle Separation between $\mathsf{StoqMA}$ and $\mathsf{MA}$
item.description: arXiv:2611.08180v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Several landmark oracle results (FOCS 2000, FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) establish strict separations along the chain $\mathsf{MA} \subseteq \mathsf{QCMA} \subseteq \mathsf{QMA}$, showing that quantum verification and quantum witnesses can each provide additional power over classical proof systems. These separations, however, use substantial coherent quantum computation, often through the quantum Fourier transform. We prove that a minimal quantum resource already suffices to outperform every classical verifier. Namely, we show the separation $$\mathsf{MA} \subsetneq \mathsf{StoqMA}$$ relative to a classical oracle. The class $\mathsf{StoqMA}$, introduced by Bravyi, Bessen, and Terhal (arXiv 2006), restricts the verifier to classical reversible computation, followed by a single Hadamard-basis measurement. Its power is closely tied to the complexity of stoquastic Hamiltonians, a sign-problem-free and seemingly more tractable class of quantum Hamiltonians. Our separating problem is to determine whether a sparse high-girth graph, given via an adjacency-list oracle, has a large or small Perron--Frobenius eigenvalue. This amounts to a ground-energy estimation task for a related stoquastic Hamiltonian. Our construction builds on a line of work on graph exploration problems with exponential quantum speedups, from welded trees (STOC 2003) to recent constructions (STOC 2021, arXiv 2026).
item.dc:creator: Yassine Hamoudi, Yvan Le Borgne, Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara

item.title: Low-Temperature Sampling via Equilibrium Disagreements
item.description: arXiv:2611.08416v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a new framework for sampling at low temperatures using Glauber dynamics. In this regime, the coexistence of competing modes (commonly referred to as phases) creates bottlenecks that can make worst-case mixing exponentially slow. The main new ingredient in our framework is to relate convergence within a phase to the geometry of disagreements between two independent configurations drawn from that phase. As applications of our approach, we consider three canonical models on random regular graphs that have been central to low-temperature sampling, and establish fast convergence from natural initialisations of Glauber dynamics for every fixed degree. We show: --- For the hard-core model on random bipartite $d$-regular graphs, Glauber dynamics initialised from either one-sided independent set mixes within the corresponding phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps throughout the non-uniqueness regime $\lambda>\lambda_c(d)$. --- For the random-cluster model on random $d$-regular graphs, for every real $q>2$, Glauber dynamics initialised from the all-in edge set mixes within the ordered phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps for all $\beta\geq \beta_c$. Similarly, Glauber dynamics initialised from the all-out edge set mixes within the disordered phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps for $\beta\leq \beta_c$. --- For the ferromagnetic Ising model on random $d$-regular graphs, Glauber dynamics initialised from all-plus or all-minus mixes within the corresponding phase in $n^{3/2+o(1)}$ steps throughout the low-temperature regime $\beta>\beta_c(d)$. We also give an $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm that combines phase samples into samples from the full distribution, avoiding in particular time-costly approximations of the corresponding partition functions to the target sampling accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Galanis, Daniel Stefankovic

item.title: Tusn\'ady's problem and online two-sample thinning
item.description: arXiv:2611.08455v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We determine the sharp order of discrepancy in Tusn\'ady's problem in every fixed dimension $d\ge 2$. The largest combinatorial discrepancy of $N$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$, extending Wei's planar result and matching Nikolov's upper bound. More strongly, with high probability, this lower bound holds simultaneously for every subset obtained by deleting at most a sufficiently small fixed fraction of a uniform $N$-point sample. We apply this geometric estimate to online thinning of two independent samples of size $n$ from an unknown common distribution, where observations must be kept or discarded upon arrival. For every fixed dimension $k\ge 1$ and expected deletion budget $\rho n$, with $0<\rho<2$, we prove that the minimax expected prefix discrepancy over lower orthants is $\Theta_{k,\rho}((\log n)^{k+1/2})$. In dimension one, the optimal terminal discrepancy is instead $\Theta_\rho((\log\log n)^{3/2})$, giving a sharp separation between the prefix and terminal objectives. For $k\ge 2$, we obtain terminal bounds differing by a factor of $\log n$. The lower bounds are based on Gaussian small-ball estimates for box-incidence matrices, while the upper bounds use stationary Metropolis thinning and, in one dimension, a terminal cancellation procedure.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Lei

item.title: Faster Linear Algebra Algorithms with Structured Random Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2508.21189v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To achieve the greatest possible speed, practitioners regularly implement randomized algorithms for low-rank approximation and least-squares regression with structured dimension reduction maps. Despite significant research effort, basic questions remain about the design and analysis of randomized linear algebra algorithms that employ structured random matrices. This paper develops a new perspective on structured dimension reduction, based on the oblivious subspace injection (OSI) property. The OSI property is a relatively weak assumption on a random matrix that holds when the matrix preserves the length of vectors on average and, with high probability, does not annihilate any vector in a low-dimensional subspace. With the OSI abstraction, the analysis of a randomized linear algebra algorithm factors into two parts: (i) proving that the algorithm works when implemented with an OSI; and (ii) proving that a given random matrix model has the OSI property. This paper develops both parts of the program. First, it analyzes standard randomized algorithms for low-rank approximation and least-squares regression under the OSI assumption. Second, it identifies many examples of OSIs, including random sparse matrices, randomized trigonometric transforms, and random matrices with tensor product structure. These theoretical results imply faster, near-optimal runtimes for several fundamental linear algebra tasks. The paper also provides guidance on implementation, along with empirical evidence that structured random matrices offer exemplary performance for a range of synthetic problems and contemporary scientific applications.
item.dc:creator: Chris Cama\~no, Ethan N. Epperly, Raphael A. Meyer, Joel A. Tropp

item.title: Computing Ultrabubbles in Linear Time by Reduction to Weak Superbubbles in the Double Covering Graph
item.description: arXiv:2605.13074v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent years, in attempts to capture variation structures in genomic and pangenomic graphs, the zoo of bubbles has been filled with more and more different variants. The first more complex variant was the superbubble which was later (informally) generalised to bidirected graphs as the ultrabubble. Ultrabubbles are more applicable in bioinformatics research, because genome and pangenome graphs usually are bidirected. In this paper, we study the relationship between superbubbles and ultrabubbles, and show that ultrabubbles in a bidirected graph are equivalent to the weak superbubbles in the corresponding double covering graph. Using this, we introduce a new linear-time algorithm to enumerate all ultrabubbles that consists of a very simple reduction to employ an existing linear-time algorithm to enumerate all weak superbubbles. Treating the superbubble algorithm as a black box, our algorithm is vastly simpler than the SPQR-tree-based linear-time ultrabubble enumeration algorithm of Sena et al. [2026]. Further, since our algorithm works on all bidirected graphs, it is strictly more powerful than the simple graph-orientation-based algorithm by Harviainen et al. [2026], which only works on a restricted class of bidirected graphs. In order to prove our equivalence, we additionally introduce simplified definitions of both ultrabubbles and weak superbubbles, through which the equivalence becomes more intuitive. Finally, our reduction motivates that some algorithmic problems in bidirected graphs can be reduced to well-known algorithmic problems in directed graphs.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Schmidt, Juha Harviainen, Corentin Moumard, Aleksandr Politov, Francisco Sena, Alexandru I. Tomescu

item.title: Space-Optimal Sensitivity Oracles for Single-Source Mincuts
item.description: arXiv:2607.00894v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How much information is needed to describe the effect of any single edge failure on all mincuts? Classical mincut representations, such as Gomory-Hu trees and cactus-like structures, show that mincuts often admit unexpectedly compact static certificates. However, much less is known about whether such compactness survives failures. We study the single-source setting. Given an undirected multigraph $G$ and source $s$, our oracle reports, for any failed edge $e$, all vertices $t$ whose $s,t$-mincut value decreases in $G\setminus{e}$; equivalently, whether $e$ belongs to some $s,t$-mincut. This is the single-source analogue of Picard-Queyranne's fixed-pair [MPS '80] and Baswana-Pandey's all-pairs sensitivity results [SODA '22], and the failure counterpart of Baswana-Gupta-Knollmann's insertion oracle [Algorithmica '22]. No subquadratic-space solution was known to date. We give an optimal $O(n)$-space oracle with $O(n)$ reporting time, matching the insertion bounds. We also give $O(n^{1.5})$-space oracles for insertions and failures, with $O(\log n)$ membership queries or amortized $O(\log^2 n)$ reporting time per affected vertex. Subquadratic-space oracles with such fast query times were unknown, even for insertions. Our main technical contribution connects farthest mincut DAGs, central to the insertion oracle, with Dinitz-Vainshtein's Connectivity Carcass for Steiner mincuts [STOC '94], which generalizes global-mincut cactus representations. These novel, intricate connections reveal the carcass's potential beyond Steiner mincuts.
item.dc:creator: Koustav Bhanja, Merav Parter, Asaf Petruschka

item.title: GPTQ-2D: Cubic-Time Two-Sided Adaptive Rounding
item.description: arXiv:2607.27042v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adaptive rounding methods such as GPTQ quantize the weights of a large language model (LLM) one at a time, propagating each rounding error to the weights not yet rounded. YAQA lowers the KL divergence from the original model with two-sided adaptive rounding under a Kronecker-factored Hessian, but its error feedback takes quartic work in the size of a square layer. We present GPTQ-2D, which provably computes the same rounding with cubic work, while still rounding the entries of each anti-diagonal in parallel. Its GPU implementation uses two levels of blocking to improve hardware utilization. We also extend the algorithm to Hessians with any number of Kronecker factors. In our experiments, GPTQ-2D is as accurate as YAQA and cuts the time to quantize Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU from 8.6 days to 1.6 hours. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/GPTQ-2D.
item.dc:creator: Jiale Chen, Torsten Hoefler, Dan Alistarh

item.title: Reportable Shortcuts with RLBWTs
item.description: arXiv:2609.06596v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Backward search over a run-length compressed Burrows-Wheeler transform (RLBWT) takes one step per pattern character, even when long stretches of the pattern match material that recurs throughout a highly repetitive collection. We describe shortcuts: for a precomputed set of pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ of strings, a backward search that has just matched $\beta$ and finds $\alpha$ immediately to its left in the pattern can cross $\alpha$ in one step. Since a shortcut is taken only after its pair has been recognized in the pattern, the search returns a report of the shortcuts it took along with the usual BWT interval. Our motivation is pangenome graphs, where such pairs mark the places where a pattern passes through a vertex, so the report gives the path a match takes through the graph. We work out the case of a single linear reference $R$, with $\beta$ ranging over the length-$\ell$ windows of $R$ starting at multiples of $\ell$, and $\alpha$ over the $2^t \ell$ characters preceding such a window. We show that the search counts correctly, that under stated conditions it crosses a stretch of the pattern matching $m$ consecutive windows of $R$ with $O(\log m + m / 2^\tau)$ shortcuts, where $2^\tau \ell$ is the longest shortcut, and that the shortcuts can be built efficiently from the RLBWT. On the Pizza&Chili cere collection of 37 genomes, shortcuts make backward search 2.3 to 4.2 times faster on exact patterns of length 200 to 1000, and 1.7 to 2.0 times faster with 1% of the characters substituted, for 86% more space. On 11 gigabases of genomes of seven bacterial species, they make it 1.6 to 1.9 times faster on exact patterns for 32% more space. On whole chromosome 19 haplotypes against 16 to 64 others from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium, shortcuts in both directions make Boyer-Moore-Li search for maximal exact matches of length at least 1000 about 8 times faster.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie

item.title: Optimal analysis of Greedy for stochastic online Euclidean matching: flat torus to the rescue
item.description: arXiv:2609.23947v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study online metric matching with $n$ servers and $n$ requests, all sampled independently and uniformly from $[0,1]^d$. We analyze the Greedy algorithm, which matches each arriving request to its closest available server. Despite its strong empirical performance, non-trivial bounds on Greedy's competitive ratio were previously known only for $d = 1$, where it is $O(1)$-competitive [BFP23]. We prove that Greedy is $O(1)$-competitive for every fixed $d\geq3$ and has competitive ratio $\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ for $d=2$. Our proof first analyzes Greedy on the flat torus and then transfers the resulting estimates to the cube.
item.dc:creator: Mingwei Yang, Sophie H. Yu

item.title: Competitive Random-Order Correlation k-Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2609.35555v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Correlation clustering has been extensively studied over the last two decades in many different computational models owing to its wide-ranging practical applications. The goal is to compute a partition of the vertex set such that the total number of disagreements, i.e. the sum of edges between clusters, and non-edges within clusters, is minimized. In this paper, we study correlation $k$-clustering, in which the total number of clusters is restricted to $k$. Correlation $k$-clustering is NP-hard, and while previous work has presented a polynomial time approximation scheme for constant $k$, there are no known results for general $k$. Our first result is a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithm for correlation $k$-clustering for general $k$. The main focus of this work is in the more challenging online setting. Noting that the best competitive ratio under adversarial arrivals is known to be $\Omega(n)$, we concentrate on the well-studied random-order model, where vertices arrive in random order and on arrival of a vertex, edges to its earlier-arrived neighbors are revealed. We prove a surprising lower bound of $\Omega(\log k)$-competitiveness for any online algorithm, which can be extended to $\Omega(\log n)$ when $k = \text{poly}(n)$. Finally, the main result of this paper is a polylogarithmic upper bound on the competitive ratio for correlation $k$-clustering, using an algorithm inspired by the classic Pivot algorithm for correlation clustering. All theorems have been verified using Lean.
item.dc:creator: Mahsa Derakhshan, Andisheh Ghasemi, Rajmohan Rajaraman, Omer Wasim, Tegan Wilson

item.title: More RLBWT Tricks
item.description: arXiv:2609.40299v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Backward search over the run-length compressed Burrows-Wheeler transform (RLBWT) of a pangenome takes one step per character of the pattern, even when long stretches of the pattern match material that occurs many times in the collection. Two-level indexing also indexes a parse of the collection, so that a search can take one step per phrase. We parse at closed syncmers, whose phrases are prefix-free, and add blocks of continuations: when each phrase of a stretch of the pattern is the smallest phrase that follows the previous one anywhere in the collection, the search crosses the whole stretch in one step, on the BWT of a sequence of block symbols. We prove that the three BWTs stay in the same order, so the search still returns exactly the BWT interval of every match, and we bound the extra space by terms that depend on the length of the collection only through the number of distinct closed syncmers. On chromosome 19 haplotypes from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium, finding the maximal exact matches of length at least 1000 of two haplotypes, on both strands, takes 5.5 to 5.7 seconds with 16, 32 or 64 other individuals, while backward search on a run-length compressed suffix array of the same collection takes 40 to 60 seconds and grows with the collection. We compare this with suffix-tree path decompositions (STPDs): over the parse, an STPD is no faster and needs about twice the memory; over the text it is about 1.7 times faster but needs the whole text in memory, about five times the space; and the published STPD-index, which compresses its text with relative Lempel-Ziv, is 8 to 10 times slower. Keeping a toehold through all three kinds of steps lets the search also list every occurrence of every MEM, for about 2 more seconds.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie

item.title: Constructive Arboricity in Almost-Linear Time for Dense Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.13937v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The arboricity of a graph is the minimum number of forests needed to partition its edges. We present an algorithm that computes the exact arboricity of a simple graph and constructs an optimal forest partition in $\min\{n^{2+o(1)},m^{4/3+o(1)}\}$ time, where $n$ and $m$ denote the numbers of vertices and edges. This improves the previous $O(m^{3/2}\log(n^2/m))$ bound of Gabow. In particular, it runs in almost-linear time, $m^{1+o(1)}$, on dense graphs with $m=\Theta(n^2)$. We also give an algorithm that constructs a partition into at most one more forest than optimal in $m^{1+o(1)}$ time. To our knowledge, it is the first almost-linear time algorithm for this problem.
item.dc:creator: Iman Gholami, Mohammad T. Hajiaghayi, Mahdi JafariRaviz, Alireza Kaviani, Soheil Mohammadkhani, AmirMohammad Shahrezaei

item.title: Greedy Region Growing: Improved Approximations for Cutwidth, Pathwidth, Flow-Expander Decomposition, and More
item.description: arXiv:2610.17237v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a new rounding technique for spreading-metric linear programs, called Greedy Region Growing, which adapts the classical technique of region growing to min-max graph layout problems and flow-expander decomposition. Using this technique, we obtain state-of-the-art approximation algorithms for several fundamental problems. (1) An $O(\log n)$-approximation for Cutwidth and Pathwidth, improving upon the previous bound of $O(\log n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})))$ due to Bansal, Katzelnick, and Schwartz (FOCS 2024). This matches the $\Omega(\log n)$ integrality gap of the standard LP relaxations. (2) An $O(\log n)$-approximation for their directed analogues, Minimum Storage and Minimum Register Sufficiency on directed acyclic graphs, improving the previous bound of $O(\log^{3/2} n)$. (3) A $\phi$-flow-expander decomposition that cuts at most an $O(\phi\log n\log\log n)$ fraction of the edges. This improves the $O(\phi\log n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})))$ bound of Bansal, Jambulapati, and Saranurak (ICALP 2026), and is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of the graph-theoretic lower bound. The vertex version of our algorithm also gives an $O(\log n)$-approximation for Treedepth. In particular, our results answer several open problems of Bansal, Katzelnick, and Schwartz (FOCS 2024). Technically, we also solve the conceptual question raised by their work: our technique shows how to adapt Seymour recursion to min-max objectives, and constructs $O(1)$-weak local partitions in spreading metrics.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Anand

item.title: Subgaussian Vector Balancing by an Ising Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.18639v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the guaranties of the Gram-Schmidt Walk Algorithm of Bansal, Dadush, Garg, and Lovett can be achieved by an Ising model. Given vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ of norm less than 1, we give a closed form for a centrally symmetric distribution on a vector $\sigma \in \{\pm 1 \}^n$ so that the signed sum $\sum_j \sigma(j) v_j$ is $1$-subgaussian. We show that the Glauber dynamics for this model mix rapidly provided that the norms of the input vectors are bounded below 1 by an inverse-polynomial. The proofs employ the theory of Lorentzian polynomials, and we use these techniques to show fast mixing bounds for other spin systems.
item.dc:creator: Heng Guo, Daniel A. Spielman, Xinyuan Zhang

item.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
item.description: arXiv:2610.25008v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $\alpha \in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+\alpha^2k^2\log(2+\alpha^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+\alpha^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $\Omega(\alpha)$ relative error. This fraction can be taken arbitrarily close to one half. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.
item.dc:creator: Edith Cohen, Uri Stemmer

item.title: Iterative Randomized Rounding for $k$-Median in General and Euclidean Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.31229v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We refine the iterative rounding framework of Byrka, Guo, Hu, Li, Wan, and Wang [FOCS'26], which gives a $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-median. Our algorithm opens $k+O(1)$ facilities with expected connection cost at most $1.9999$ times the standard LP value. Despite the small numerical gain, this shows that the LP integrality gap is below $2$ with a constant additive facility allowance, partially answering Li and Svensson's open question [SICOMP'16]. Their reduction yields a $1.9999$-approximation opening at most $k$ facilities. Our preprocessing makes the LP solution $\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)$-integral with a $(1+\varepsilon)$ loss in each client's expected connection cost and $O(1)$ extra facilities, without special treatment of clients with concentrated fractional facilities. We replace batch processing with single-facility openings and combine a tighter analysis for clients with unequal distances to their facilities with a complementary algorithm for nearly uniform distances. In Euclidean metrics, we obtain a $1.71955$-approximation for $k$-median and a $1.4561$-approximation for uncapacitated facility location (UFL). For every $p\ge2$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain a $((3^p+2)/3+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-clustering with $p$-th power distance costs. For $p=2$, our $(11/3+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-means improves the $(3+\ln2+\varepsilon)$ bound of Anand, Charikar, Cohen-Addad, Gao, Grandoni, Lee, Sharma, and van Wijland [SODA'27]. The Euclidean $k$-median, $k$-means, and UFL ratios are below the respective general-metric hardness bounds $1+2/e$, $1+8/e$ [STOC'02], and $1.463$ [J. Algorithms'99]. The Euclidean $k$-median bound relies on a geometric inequality proved via a nonnegativity certificate constructed from positive-semidefinite kernels.
item.dc:creator: Jaros{\l}aw Byrka, Yuhao Guo, Yang S. Hu, Shi Li, Yongho Shin, Phanu Vajanopath, Chengzhang Wan, Zaixuan Wang

item.title: Santa Claus and Weighted Nash Social Welfare with Subadditive Valuations
item.description: arXiv:2611.05229v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study max-min allocation (the Santa Claus problem) and weighted Nash social welfare for $n$ agents with subadditive valuations over $m$ indivisible items. Using demand queries, we give randomized polynomial-time approximation algorithms with factors $O(\sqrt n)$ and $O(\Gamma(w))$, respectively, where $\Gamma(w)=\exp((\ln n-H(w))/2)$ and $H(w)=-\sum_i w_i\ln w_i$ for positive weights summing to one. Both ratios are independent of $m$. The max-min result improves the $2n-1$ bound of Khot and Ponnuswami (2007). We also give simpler $O(\sqrt n)$ algorithms for additive valuations and for submodular valuations with value queries, improving the $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ bound of Saha and Srinivasan (2018) in the additive case. For Nash welfare, $\Gamma(w)=1$ for equal weights and $\Gamma(w)\le\sqrt n$ in general. We prove a configuration-LP integrality gap of $\Theta(\Gamma(w))$ for every prescribed weight vector, even for XOS valuations. For every fixed $D>0$, we also prove information-theoretic approximation lower bounds of $\Omega_D(\sqrt{n/\ln n})$ and $\Omega_D(\Gamma(w)/\sqrt{\ln n})$, respectively, for randomized algorithms making at most $n^D$ adaptive queries. These hold on XOS instances with $m=\Theta(n)$ items, even with simultaneous access to value, demand, and XOS supporting-clause oracles. They apply both to guarantees with success probability at least $2/3$ and to guarantees in expected welfare. The weighted bound holds for every prescribed weight vector and is vacuous below one. Thus the oracle lower bounds are within an $O(\sqrt{\ln n})$ factor of our upper bounds, while the configuration-LP gaps match them up to constants. Our algorithms build on random matchings for large items and charge the aggregate loss across configurations to the at most $n$ matched items.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Chen, Yuda Feng, Weijiang Hu, Shi Li, Ruilong Zhang

item.title: Parameterized Complexity of Fair Vertex Evaluation Problems
item.description: arXiv:1803.06878v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph modification problems form a unifying framework for many classical graph problems, where the goal is to remove a minimum number of vertices so that the resulting graph satisfies a desired property $\pi$. In this work, we replace the classical objective of minimizing the solution size with the fair objective [Lin&Sahni: Fair edge deletion problems. IEEE Trans. Comput. 89], which minimizes the maximum number of deleted neighbors incident to any vertex. This fairness criterion aims to distribute deletions evenly across the graph and leads to new algorithmic and complexity challenges. We study fair deletion and evaluation problems in the logical setting, where the target property~$\pi$ is defined by a formula in a logic $\mathsf{L}$. In particular, we consider the Fair $\mathsf{L}$ Vertex Evaluation problem, which asks whether there exists a vertex set $W$ of bounded fair cost such that a given formula $\varphi(X)$ holds in the input graph $G$. Our main result is an FPT algorithm for the Fair MSO$_1$ Vertex Evaluation problem with one free variable, parameterized by the twin cover number of the input graph and the quantifier length of the formula. We further show that extending this result to formulas with $\ell$ free variables is unlikely: the $\ell$-Fair FO Vertex Evaluation problem is W[1]-hard for parameter $\ell$ even on graphs of twin cover one. As a concrete case study, we investigate the Fair Vertex Cover}\ problem, one of the simplest fairness-aware graph problems. We prove that it is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the combined treedepth and feedback vertex set, but admits an FPT algorithm for the parameter modular width.
item.dc:creator: Du\v{s}an Knop, Tom\'a\v{s} Masa\v{r}\'ik, Tom\'a\v{s} Toufar

item.title: A Strongly Polynomial-Time 7/9-Approximation Algorithm for Maximin Share Allocations
item.description: arXiv:2511.13056v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study maximin share (MMS) allocations of indivisible goods under nonnegative additive valuations. We give a strongly polynomial-time algorithm that allocates to every agent a bundle worth at least $7/9$ of her MMS, improving the previous $10/13$ guarantee of Heidari et al. (SODA 2026). Our analysis uses a dynamic witness-allocation framework that tracks the remaining goods from each agent's perspective throughout the allocation process. We obtain the computational result by iteratively refining upper bounds on MMS values, using only polynomially many runs of the allocation algorithm. Finally, we formalize and verify our main results in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Xin Huang, Shengwei Zhou

item.title: Dequantization Barriers for Guided Stoquastic Hamiltonians
item.description: arXiv:2602.23183v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct a probability distribution, induced by the Perron--Frobenius eigenvector of an exponentially large graph, that cannot be efficiently sampled by any classical algorithm, even when given the best-possible warm-start distribution. In the quantum setting, this problem can be viewed as preparing the ground state of a stoquastic Hamiltonian given a guiding state as input, and is known to be efficiently solvable on a quantum computer. We further show that even estimating the ground-state energy of that Hamiltonian remains classically hard. Our results suggest that no efficient classical algorithm can solve a broad class of stoquastic ground-state problems. Our graph is constructed from a class of high-degree, high-girth spectral expanders (such as the LPS Ramanujan graphs) to which self-similar trees are attached. This builds on and extends prior work of Gily\'en, Hastings, and Vazirani (Quantum 2021, STOC 2021), which ruled out dequantization for a specific stoquastic adiabatic path algorithm. We strengthen their result by ruling out any classical algorithm for guided ground-state preparation or energy estimation, while also providing a derandomized construction.
item.dc:creator: Yassine Hamoudi, Yvan Le Borgne, Shrinidhi Teganahally Sridhara
